resources.string: A -O cable has no green-and-yellow core, and its cores must never be pressed into service as a protective conductor by colouring one of them. If the cable does not have the conductor, it is the wrong cable.
H07V-U and NYY-J read position by position, not from a table.
Harmonised · 450/750 V · PVC insulated · solid conductor. The single core pulled into conduit on almost every installation.
VDE type · PVC · single core, no sheath · fine-stranded. Panel wiring, where it has to bend.
VDE type · PVC insulated · sheathed installation cable · with a green-and-yellow. The grey flat cable clipped to a wall.
VDE type · PVC insulated · PVC sheathed · with a green-and-yellow. The black cable used for buried and outdoor runs.

A cable designation is not an arbitrary part number — every letter and digit stands for a property, in a fixed order. Once the positions are known the code reads itself, which is why this page decodes the scheme rather than listing products.
Identification by colour, current and superseded
Blue with green-yellow ends, or the reverse
Still present in installed plant. The overlap is the danger: old red is line, new red is nothing, and old black is neutral while new black is a line conductor. Never assume — always prove dead.
The NEC mandates only the grounded (white or grey) and grounding (green) conductors; phase colours are convention, not code, and vary between installations.
Low enough that no meaningful voltage can appear across it, typically well under 0.05 Ω
What to measure before energising, in what order, and what reading to accept.

Measured between live conductors, and between live conductors and earth. A reading that is merely above the minimum but far below the rest of the installation is worth investigating; degradation shows up as a trend before it shows up as a failure.
Agrees with the calculated value for the length and section installed
Proves the mechanism, not the installation. It injects a current inside the device and says nothing about whether the earth is connected.
The five-times test is not a formality. A device can pass at its rated residual current and still be too slow where it matters, which is a large fault on a wet floor.
The order, and why it is an order

The dead tests come first, and not for tidiness. Each one is checking for a condition that makes the next step dangerous, so taking them out of order means energising something you have not yet proved is safe to energise.

Insulation testing applies hundreds of volts DC. Anything with electronics in it — dimmers, drives, LED drivers, surge protection — must be disconnected first, or the test destroys it. This is the single most expensive mistake on this page.
Inspect before measuring anything: connections tight, correct devices fitted, protective conductors present and identified.
Continuity of protective conductors and of any bonding. A broken earth invalidates every test after it.
Continuity of ring final circuits, where the installation has them.
Insulation resistance, with the circuit dead and electronic equipment disconnected.
Polarity: every switch and every protective device in the line conductor, never in the neutral.
Energise. Everything from here on is a live test.
Earth fault loop impedance, and compare it against the maximum the device allows.
RCD operating times, at the rated residual current and at five times it.
Phase sequence, before any three-phase machine is run for the first time.
Below the maximum the protective device allows, corrected for temperature

The device must interrupt the maximum prospective fault current at its position — use the short-circuit calculator for that figure. A breaker asked to break more than its rating does not merely fail; it fails destructively.
B, C and D characteristics and breaking capacity
Domestic, well away from the transformer

The band is a range, not a point: a Type C is guaranteed not to trip below 5 × In and guaranteed to trip above 10 × In. Between the two it may or may not. Any calculation that has to be safe uses the upper figure, which is what the earth fault loop calculator does.
Must not trip within one hour

The thermal element protects the cable against sustained overload; the magnetic element protects it against a fault. A breaker that never trips magnetically is not protecting the circuit against a short — it is only waiting for the bimetal.
Soil thermal resistivity, depth of burial and direct sunlight each carry their own factor and none of them is here. A buried run needs its own corrections from the standard.
The ambient and grouping figures the cable calculator applies.

The two factors are applied together, not the worse of the two. A cable in 40 °C air with six circuits bunched around it keeps 0.87 × 0.57 — half its tabulated rating — and neither factor on its own looks alarming.
Read from the same table the calculator uses, so the two cannot disagree. Values between the steps are interpolated linearly, which is accepted practice.
Arrangement 1: cables bunched in air, on a surface, embedded or enclosed. Spacing the cables by one diameter recovers most of this, which is what a wider tray buys you.
Four faults you will actually be called out to, and the order to eliminate causes in.
An MCB trips with a normal load
Trips instantly on switch-on: inrush. A transformer, a motor or a bank of LED drivers wants a Type C or D, not a Type B.
Trips after several minutes: thermal. The load is genuinely near the rating, or the breaker is hot.
A hot consumer unit. Breakers derate with temperature, and a board full of them in a warm cupboard runs well above room ambient.
Neighbouring circuits loaded at the same time. Heat from the breakers either side is enough to shift the thermal characteristic.
Harmonic current. An RMS-reading clamp shows more than a mean-reading one, and the breaker responds to the real heating.
A genuine intermittent short — a screw through a cable, a chafed strand — which shows as an instant trip that will not reset.
Establish whether it trips instantly or after a while. Instant is magnetic and means current; delayed is thermal and means heat.
Unbalanced supply. A few percent of voltage unbalance produces many times that in current unbalance, and the extra current is all heat.
Single phasing. One phase lost, the motor still turns, and the remaining two carry far more than their rating.
Mechanical overload, or a driven machine that has stiffened. Current is high and balanced.
Low terminal voltage. The motor draws more current for the same torque, so a voltage drop problem arrives disguised as a heating problem.
Blocked ventilation, or an ambient hotter than the motor is rated for. Check the fan cover before the windings.
Too many starts per hour. Starting current is several times full load and the heat has nowhere to go between starts.
Bearing wear or shaft misalignment. Usually audible, and usually accompanied by vibration.
Measure all three line currents before touching anything. The comparison between them eliminates half of this list in one reading.
Accumulated standing leakage. Every electronic supply leaks a little to earth; enough of them on one 30 mA device adds up to a trip with nothing actually faulty.
A drive or an EMC filter. These leak by design, and the leakage is high-frequency — which a Type AC device may not even measure correctly.
Moisture in an outdoor circuit or a buried joint. Classically trips after rain and clears by afternoon.
The wrong RCD type for the load. A drive needs Type B; single-phase electronics need at least Type A.
A borrowed neutral between two circuits. Current returns through the wrong RCD and the imbalance is real.
Genuine insulation failure. Test it, rather than assuming it, because it is the least common of these and the only one worth replacing cable for.
Split the load before you replace anything. Half the circuits off, test, then halve again — it costs four operations to find the offender and no parts.
Voltage is low at the load
Low only under load, recovering when the load is removed: a voltage drop problem. Measure at the origin and at the load and work along the run.
Low everywhere including at rest: the supply itself, or a transformer tap. Not a problem inside the installation.
Low on one phase only: a loose or corroded connection on that phase. Thermal imaging finds these in seconds.
Voltage low on one phase and high on another: a lost neutral. This is urgent — single-phase loads are being fed line-to-line.
Momentary dips when a large motor starts: the starting current, not a fault. Consider a soft starter or a stiffer supply.
First establish whether it is low under load or low at rest. That one question separates a cable problem from a supply problem.

This is the practical difference between the systems. A TN loop is low enough for the overcurrent device to see a fault; a TT loop runs through the ground and is not, which is why a TT installation depends on an RCD. An IT system does not disconnect on the first fault at all — it alarms, and the second fault is the dangerous one.
TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT and IT
Supply isolated or earthed through an impedance
Hospitals, ships, processes that must not stop
Insulation monitor alarms; first fault is tolerated
The first letter describes the supply, the second the installation. Everything else about the system follows from those two decisions.
Exposed parts earthed via the supply
Overcurrent device, on the low loop impedance
No RCD is possible; not permitted for final circuits
PEN to the origin, separated after it
Very common; a lost PEN raises every earthed metal part
Low loop impedance; a broken PE is not disguised
Own earth electrode, independent of the supply
Rural supplies and anywhere the PEN cannot be trusted
RCD — the loop through earth is far too high
Every equation the app applies, on one page.
Symbols are defined on each calculator's own formula card. This page is for recognising an equation, not for working one out from scratch.
The note gives the test hammer: its mass and the drop height that delivers the stated energy. IK08 and above are what a car park or a school corridor asks for.
A digit replaced by X means that protection is not specified, not that it is absent — IPX4 says nothing about dust.
The levels are not cumulative above 6: an IP×7 enclosure is not necessarily protected against jets. Where both matter the rating is written IP×6/IP×7.
High-pressure hot water jets. IEC 60529 calls this the ninth level; equipment is marked IP69K, which is ISO 20653's name for the same test.

These are the values the app calculates with, not a separate table — a figure quoted here cannot drift away from the one the cable calculators use. Correct for temperature: ρ(θ) = ρ₂₀ · [1 + α₂₀ · (θ − 20)].
If you find one of these on an existing installation, assume it is not the only one. They cluster: whoever made this decision made the others too.
Errors that pass inspection, work for years, and then do not.
Every item here produces an installation that works. That is exactly the problem: nothing complains, the job is signed off, and the defect waits for the one condition that turns it into an incident.
Why these are the dangerous ones
Neutral and protective conductor swapped, or bonded downstream of the origin. Everything works until a fault, and then exposed metal is live.
A test result recorded from the wrong circuit. The paperwork then certifies a circuit nobody measured.
A borrowed neutral between two circuits. Isolating one circuit leaves its neutral live from the other, and the RCD sees an imbalance that is real.
A protective conductor sized by eye. It has to survive the fault, not merely be present — that is the adiabatic check, and it is the one nobody does.
Aluminium conductor into a terminal rated for copper. The joint creeps, warms, oxidises and eventually arcs.
A Type AC RCD in front of a drive. It cannot correctly measure the leakage the drive produces, so it may not operate at all.
The PEN conductor split into N and PE at more than one point on a TN-C-S supply, or split at all on a TT one.
Power and data cables run touching for a long parallel section. Works on the bench and produces intermittent data faults on site.
Cable sized on current alone for a long run, or on voltage drop alone for a short one. Both constraints apply to every circuit.
A conductor derated on paper but not in the enclosure it actually sits in. Grouping and ambient are properties of the installation, not of the drawing.

These are indicative figures for estimating, not values from a standard. Use the nameplate or a measurement for anything being designed or billed — an induction motor's power factor collapses at part load, which is exactly when it is easiest to get wrong.
A bonding conductor is not a protective conductor and cannot be borrowed as one. If a fault current ever has to flow through it, it was the wrong conductor.
Two different jobs that share a colour and are constantly confused.

A protective conductor exists to carry fault current back to the source so a device operates. A bonding conductor exists so that two things a person can touch at once cannot sit at different voltages. The first solves the fault; the second makes the fault survivable while it lasts.

This is why a supplementary bonding conductor can be small and still correct. It is not sized to carry a fault; it is sized so the resistance between the two parts keeps the touch voltage below 50 V while the protective device does its work.
Carries fault current to the source
Ties incoming services to the earth bar

A single-core armoured cable must not have its steel armour magnetically closed around one conductor alone — the circulating current heats the armour. Aluminium armour, or all cores in one armour, is why the rule exists.
Every layer, and the job it is doing.

Everything outside the conductor exists to keep the conductor where it is, insulated from what it must not touch, and intact for as long as the installation lasts. When a cable fails it is almost never the copper.
Withstands the voltage, sets the temperature rating
Makes the cable round so the sheath can be extruded
Steel wire, or aluminium on single core
Takes mechanical damage; often the earth path
Contains the electric field, drains interference
Not insulation, and never treated as such
A K-factor or K-rated transformer is built to survive harmonic heating, not to remove it. The harmonics are still in the cable and still in the neutral.
Why a neutral can carry more than any line, and what THD is actually telling you.

On a balanced three-phase system the fundamental currents cancel in the neutral, which is why the neutral is often the smallest conductor in the cable. The third harmonic and its multiples do not: they arrive in phase with each other and add up. A supply feeding banks of switched-mode power supplies can put more current in the neutral than in any line.

That is a sizing problem before it is a power-quality problem. IEC 60364-5-52 requires the neutral to be counted as a loaded conductor once third-harmonic content passes 15 %, and the cable derated accordingly — which is a smaller cable carrying a larger current if nobody checked.
The third harmonic does not cancel

A THD of 40 % on a circuit drawing 2 A is nothing; the same figure on a 200 A feeder is a transformer problem. Current THD is a ratio, so it says how distorted the current is and not how much distorted current there is. Ask for the amps.
What THD does not tell you
Opening an Ex d enclosure in a live hazardous area removes exactly the property the certification is about. Only Ex i circuits may be worked on live.
Zones, protection types, and what the marking on the enclosure means.

Nothing about the equipment can be chosen until the area has been classified. The zone states how often an explosive atmosphere is present, and that decides the equipment category — not the other way round. Classification is a specialist activity and this page is an orientation, not a substitute for it.
Present continuously or for long periods
Unlikely, and brief if it happens
Present continuously or for long periods
Unlikely, and brief if it happens
Increased safety — no arcs or hot surfaces
The only type safe to work on live
Intrinsically safe — energy limited below ignition
What each field on a motor or transformer plate is conditional on.

A nameplate is not a list of properties, it is a list of guarantees under stated conditions. The current is at that voltage, that frequency, that duty and that ambient. Change any one and the number stops applying — which is why a 400 V motor on a 380 V supply draws more current, not less.
Input is higher by the efficiency
S1 continuous; anything else is not
Headroom, not a rating to run at
Sets the fault current it can deliver
Must match to parallel two units
Dips, swells, flicker and unbalance: what causes them and what they break.

A voltage dip is almost always a large load starting or a fault clearing somewhere on the network — yours or a neighbour's. It lasts cycles, not seconds, and the equipment that notices is the equipment with a contactor: the coil drops out at around 70 % and the process stops even though nothing was damaged.
Most of it is somebody else's motor
Large load switched off, unbalanced fault

A few percent of voltage unbalance produces several times that in current unbalance in an induction motor, and all of the extra current becomes heat in the rotor. It is the quietest of these faults and the one that shortens machine life without ever tripping anything.
A selectivity claim without a manufacturer's table behind it is a hope. Two curves that look clear on a log plot are the most common way that hope is formed.
Making only the nearest device open, and knowing when you cannot.

Selectivity is achieved by current, by time, or by energy. Current works while the fault current at the downstream device is well below the upstream device's instantaneous threshold. Time works by delaying the upstream trip. Energy — total selectivity at high fault currents — cannot be reasoned about from curves at all and exists only in the manufacturer's tested tables.

Two breakers whose curves merely do not cross are not selective. Near the origin both devices are in their instantaneous region, both open in milliseconds, and the curves say nothing about which got there first.
Fails once the fault reaches the upstream instantaneous band
Ratio of ratings, typically 1:1.6 or better
Costs let-through energy on every fault
Upstream delayed by 100 ms or more
Valid only for the exact pair listed
Temperature rise, forms of separation, and why a board fails its type test.

Devices are rated in open air at 30 or 40 °C. Inside a closed board they heat each other, and the rated diversity factor of the assembly — not the sum of the device ratings — is what the board can actually carry. A board that adds up on paper can still fail its temperature rise verification.
Units separated from each other, terminals not
Lets one circuit be worked on live
Units and their terminals all separated

IEC 61439 verifies the design, not the individual board: temperature rise, short-circuit withstand, insulation, protective circuit continuity and IP. Substituting a device for an equivalent one from another maker voids the verification, however similar the datasheet looks.
What Dyn11 says, and what has to match before two units run in parallel.

The capital letter is the high-voltage winding, the small letter the low. D is delta, Y is star, z is zigzag; an n means the star point is brought out as a neutral. The number is the phase shift in units of 30°, read as a clock face — 11 means the low-voltage side leads by 30°.
Delta HV, star LV with neutral, 30° lead
Regional preference; will not parallel with Dyn11

Four things must agree: the vector group, the voltage ratio, the impedance voltage, and the phase sequence. Mismatched uk means the transformers do not share the load in proportion to their ratings — the stiffer one takes more and overheats first.

Both conditions must hold. The first sizes the device between the load and the cable. The second says the device must actually operate before the cable is damaged — for a modern breaker it is satisfied by construction, but for some fuses it is not, and it has to be checked.
Standard device sizes and the coordination rule
Design current ≤ device rating ≤ cable capacity

A gG fuse protects against both overload and short circuit. An aM fuse protects only against short circuit and must be paired with a separate overload device — substituting one for the other leaves a motor with no overload protection at all.
Operating current must not exceed 1.45 × cable capacity
Fire protection on a distribution board
No longer accepted in many countries
Three-phase drives, EV chargers, PV inverters
Which residual waveform each type can detect
30 mA is protection against electric shock; 300 mA is protection against fire. They are different jobs, and one does not replace the other.

Selectivity between two RCDs needs more than different ratings: the upstream device must also be an S type, whose deliberate delay lets the downstream one clear first. Two instantaneous devices in series will trip together.
Each type detects everything the ones above it do, and one thing more. The failure is silent: an RCD facing a residual current it cannot see does not trip and gives no indication that it is blind.
Disconnect completely. Every source, including any that back-feeds — generators, UPS, PV, capacitors.
Secure against re-connection. Lock off and label; a note alone is not a lock.
Verify that the installation is dead. Prove the tester on a known source, test the circuit, then prove the tester again.
Earth and short-circuit. Required on high voltage; good practice wherever a supply could return.
Protect against adjacent live parts. Cover or barrier anything still energised within reach.
Proving the tester before and after is not ceremony. A tester that failed during the check reads dead on a live circuit, and the reading you trusted was the failure.
Before working on anything you intend to treat as dead.
The order is the rule. Each step assumes the one before it was completed, and the third exists because the first two can both be done perfectly on the wrong circuit.
A flooded bank vents hydrogen while charging. That is a ventilation requirement and an ignition-source exclusion zone, not a preference.
What each chemistry costs over its life, not on the invoice.

Two banks of the same amp-hours are not the same purchase. Usable depth and cycle life decide how much energy you actually get out over ten years, and on that measure the cheapest bank is rarely the cheapest.
Tolerant warm, must not charge below 0 °C
A cable rated for a wet location is not the same as one rated for permanent immersion, and neither is the same as one rated for burial. Read the sheath specification, not the insulation.
What the route does to the cable, and which construction survives it.

Section and insulation answer how much current and how hot. They say nothing about being buried in wet ground, dragged along a cable chain a million times, or asked to keep a smoke extract fan running while the building burns. Those are construction questions, and picking the wrong construction is a fault that arrives years later.
Armoured, XLPE, with a sheath rated for wet
Ground movement and stones; the armour is the mechanical protection and the earth path
Supported along its length, so only handling and sunlight matter
Water tracks along a sheath that was only rated for damp
Must keep the circuit alive while people leave, and must not add smoke
Double-insulated, UV and ozone rated, 1.5 kV
Outdoors for 25 years at a voltage ordinary cable is not rated for
Fatigue, not current, is what ends it; a solid conductor work-hardens and breaks
Salt, vibration and a fire nobody can walk away from
The second digit is not cumulative above 6. IPX7 (immersion) does not imply IPX5 (jets); an enclosure that needs both is marked with both.
What the environment demands, room by room.

An enclosure is chosen for the cleaning regime and the weather, not for the day it was installed. A panel that never sees rain still sees a pressure washer once a year, and that is the rating it needs.
An LSZH cable is chosen for the people evacuating through the smoke, not for the cable. Where a building has one escape route, it stops being a preference.
Temperature, fire behaviour, flexibility and price, and what each buys.

XLPE carries more current than PVC in the same section because it tolerates a hotter conductor. That extra current is real, but so is the stiffer cable, the larger bending radius and the terminal that now has to survive 90 °C.
A higher rating is not free
Aluminium into a terminal rated for copper is the failure this comparison exists to prevent. The joint creeps, warms, oxidises, and eventually arcs — years after the person who made it has left.
Where aluminium saves money, and where it costs more than it saves.

Aluminium needs roughly one and a half times the section for the same current, and still weighs about half as much. On a long heavy feeder that is a saving in both money and installation effort. On a 2.5 mm² final circuit there is nothing to save and a termination to get wrong.
Two sizes larger, one third the weight
Bimetallic lug, correct torque, re-check after settling
Long feeders, risers, from about 35 mm² up
IEC 60228 and the app's own material data
Ratings are a separate question from type. 30 mA protects people, 100 and 300 mA protect against fire, and 10 mA is used where the risk is high and the circuit is small.
The type is decided by the shape of the leakage, not by its size.
An RCD can only trip on current it can measure. Put a Type AC in front of a drive and it may never see the DC-biased leakage the drive produces — the device is present, tested, and blind.
Match the type to the load
Three-phase drives, EV chargers, PV inverters
A drive is not only a starting method. If the load ever runs at part speed it pays for itself in energy, and a fan at 80 % speed draws about half the power.
What each method costs you in current, in torque and in money.

Every method here works by reducing the voltage, and torque falls with the square of it. Where the reduction is a change of connection or a transformer — star-delta, autotransformer — the line current falls in the same proportion as the torque: star applies 58 % of the voltage, so a third of the current buys a third of the torque. A soft starter drops the voltage in series instead, so its current falls with the voltage and its torque with the square — two-thirds of the current leaves under half the torque. Either way, a loaded conveyor that starts fine direct-on-line may not start at all in star.
Torque is what you give up
Voltage dip on the whole board
Bypass contactor needed for continuous running
A map of the documents this app follows.

Most low-voltage installation questions are answered inside IEC 60364, and the part number says which chapter. Knowing that -4-41 is protection and -5-52 is wiring systems turns a search into a lookup.
The 60364 series is a book in parts
Protection against electric shock; disconnection times
Wiring systems; current capacity and correction factors
Special installations — bathrooms, marinas, PV, medical
The symbols that differ between the two conventions, and the ones that trip people.

Most symbols are the same in both conventions — a motor is a circle with an M in either. Only the ones that genuinely differ are here, because a chart padded with identical rows is a chart nobody finishes reading.
IEC and ANSI side by side
One winding, tapped. There is no isolation between the two sides.
The crosses mark a device that breaks fault current. That is what separates it from the two above.
The operating coil of a relay or contactor; its contacts are drawn elsewhere on the sheet.
The arc points the way the delay acts. Facing the movement means the delay is on closing.
The bar across the contact is the only difference from the one above, and it inverts the circuit.
Open at rest, closes when operated.
Made to switch load current repeatedly, and to drop out when its coil loses supply.
Contacts, coils and instruments as a control schematic shows them.
Drawn to IEC 60617; designations from IEC 81346
These are drawn from the geometric description in IEC 60617, not reproduced from it. Where your local drawing office uses a variant, the local convention wins.
Sits in series with the line. Its secondary must never be left open while primary current flows.
Isolates only. It must never be opened under load — it has nothing to quench the arc.
The bar marks a maintained supply — it stays lit when the mains goes.
Mushroom head, latching, normally closed. It has to break the circuit by positive opening.
The dot is the whole difference. Without it the lines cross without touching.

A schematic labels its devices with a letter and a number — -Q1, -F2, -K3. The letter is an IEC 81346 reference designation and says what role the device plays, which is the half of the meaning a symbol shape does not carry.
What the letter on a device means
The curved plate is the ANSI mark for a polarised capacitor. IEC draws both plates straight and marks polarity separately.
The ANSI breaker is a blade with a quarter-arc. To an IEC eye it reads as a switch, which is the expensive misreading on this page.
ANSI marks the fixed contacts with small circles and draws the circuit horizontally; IEC draws it vertically.
IEC stacks three shortening bars; ANSI draws a rake. Both mean the same connection.
Nothing alike. An ANSI fuse is a slender loop; an IEC fuse is a box with a line through it.
The one everybody knows. IEC draws a plain box, ANSI a zigzag.
IEC draws two overlapping circles, ANSI two coils facing a core.
Outlets, switches and luminaires as a floor plan shows them.

A single-line diagram says how the circuit connects; a plan says where the apparatus is. That is why most of these sit on a short wall stub — it orients the symbol and says which surface the fitting is mounted on.
A plan is not a circuit
Residual current and overcurrent in one pole. The extra trip element is the difference from an RCD.
Residual current only. It needs a separate device for overload and short circuit.
The line across the box separates AC from DC; the flat side of the diagonal is the DC side.
Power apparatus as a distribution drawing shows it, with the designation letters.
Drawn to IEC 60617; designations from IEC 81346
The bar across the throat is the earth contact.
Limits transient overvoltage. It has no role in overcurrent or fault protection.
The half-circle is arc quenching. It can break load current, but not fault current.
Goes between a pair of two-way switches to add a third control point.
Two of these control one point from two places.
Protects the motor against sustained overload. It is not short-circuit protection.
Sits across the line, not in series with it. That is the drawing difference from a current transformer.
How fast a fault must be cleared
Distribution circuits, and final circuits above those ratings
Longer times are accepted here because nobody is expected to be holding a distribution cable. The relaxation does not extend to the final circuits fed from it.
Final circuits — sockets to 63 A, fixed equipment to 32 A
The times shorten as the voltage rises, because the current through a body rises with it. A TT system is given less time than TN at the same voltage since the touch voltage during a fault is higher.
Written phase-to-neutral / phase-to-phase. 230/400 V and 120/240 V describe the same three-phase four-wire arrangement at different sizes.
Europe, most of Asia and Africa
The drop limits are from IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G and are measured from the origin of the installation to the load. They are a recommendation the local code may tighten.
